definition: The part of a protocol stack that provides communication between application endpoints. TCP and UDP use port numbers to multiplex flows; TCP adds an ordered reliable byte stream, while QUIC supplies transport services above UDP.
example: TCP, UDP and QUIC are all transport protocols; IP below them only moves packets from host to host.

definition: The useful bytes a packet, segment, frame or record carries, as opposed to headers, tags and other overhead that describe or route it.
example: A 1,500-byte IPv4 packet carrying TCP has 20 bytes of IP header, 20 bytes of TCP header and up to 1,460 bytes of payload.

definition: One end of a network conversation: a particular host's IP address and port, or the program using it. A TCP connection joins exactly two endpoints.
example: In a connection from 198.51.100.7:51000 to 203.0.113.5:443, each address-and-port pair is an endpoint.

definition: Sharing one resource among many users. At the transport layer it means many applications on a host sending through one IP address, told apart by port numbers; HTTP/2 also multiplexes many requests over one connection.
example: A browser, a game and a DNS lookup can all send from the same IP address at once because each uses its own port.

definition: Handing each arriving packet to the right application. The kernel reads the transport header (ports, and for TCP the full 5-tuple) to choose the receiving socket.
example: An arriving UDP datagram for port 53 is demultiplexed to the DNS server's socket.

definition: A 16-bit number (0 to 65,535) in the TCP or UDP header that identifies which program on a host should get the data. The source port identifies the sender's end and the destination port the receiver's.
example: HTTPS servers listen on port 443; a browser connecting to one usually sends from a temporary port such as 51000.

definition: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority: the body that keeps the official registries of protocol numbers, including which port numbers are assigned to which services.
example: IANA lists port 22 for SSH and port 443 for HTTPS.

definition: A port number from 0 to 1023, which IANA calls system ports. They are assigned to standard services, and on Unix-like systems binding to them traditionally needs administrator rights.
example: 22 (SSH), 53 (DNS) and 443 (HTTPS) are well-known ports.

definition: A port number from 1024 to 49151, which IANA calls user ports. Services can register these for their own use without special privileges.
example: MySQL uses 3306 and PostgreSQL uses 5432, both registered ports.

definition: A port number from 49152 to 65535, which IANA reserves for temporary, automatically allocated use and never assigns to services.
example: IANA's dynamic range holds 16,384 ports; Linux uses its own, larger default range instead.

definition: A temporary local port selected for a socket, often automatically for a client. Allocation, release and reuse depend on protocol, endpoint tuple, retained connection state and operating-system policy; the documented Linux default allocation range is 32768–60999.
example: Linux picks ephemeral ports from 32768 to 60999 by default, 28,232 numbers in all.

definition: The Linux setting that sets the range of local ports the kernel picks ephemeral ports from. Its default is 32768 to 60999.
example: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range prints the current range, for example 32768 60999.

definition: Running out of free source ports when one client makes many connections to the same destination, because only the source port can differ between them. New connections then fail until ports are freed.
example: With one source address, one fixed destination and no early tuple reuse, 600 connections/s each occupying a tuple for 60 s would need 36,000 tuples.

definition: A port below an operating-system privilege threshold, traditionally 1024 on Unix-like systems. Linux makes the first unprivileged port configurable per network namespace, and CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE grants the relevant bind privilege; a low port does not authenticate a service.
example: A Linux namespace using threshold 1024 requires suitable privilege to bind port 443.

definition: A Linux capability granting permission to bind Internet-domain sockets to privileged ports. The traditionally privileged range is below 1024, but the threshold is configurable in a network namespace.
example: Granting CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to a web server binary lets it listen on port 80 as an ordinary user.

definition: A Linux feature that gives a group of processes its own private copy of the network stack: its own interfaces, routing table, ports and settings. Containers use it so each gets its own network view.
example: Two containers can both listen on port 80 because each has its own network namespace.

definition: A way of representing and adding binary numbers in which a carry out of the top bit is added back in at the bottom. The Internet checksum is the one's complement of the one's-complement sum of the data's 16-bit words.
example: In 16-bit one's-complement addition, 0xFFFF + 0x0001 wraps round to 0x0001 rather than 0x0000.

definition: IP-layer information included in a TCP or UDP checksum calculation but not transmitted as part of the transport header. Source/destination addresses, protocol and transport length help detect accidental misdelivery; checksum collisions remain possible and this is not authentication.
example: Changing the destination address changes checksum input, although collisions mean this is not a perfect misdelivery test.

definition: An IPv6 packet whose payload exceeds 65,535 bytes, represented with a Jumbo Payload option under RFC 2675. UDP uses a zero length field for a UDP packet longer than 65,535 bytes in this mode; normal path and implementation support cannot be assumed.
example: RFC 2675 allows a UDP packet longer than 65,535 bytes to use zero in its UDP length field.

definition: A Linux/POSIX error code meaning 'message too long': the datagram is bigger than the socket or path allows, so the send fails locally instead of the packet being fragmented.
example: Sending a 9,000-byte UDP datagram with path MTU discovery on a 1,500-byte path can fail with EMSGSIZE.

definition: The 16-bit UDP field counting header plus data in bytes: normally 8–65,535. RFC 2675 defines the IPv6 jumbogram exception, using zero when the UDP packet exceeds the ordinary limit.
example: A UDP datagram carrying 100 bytes of data has a length field of 108.

definition: The five values that identify a TCP connection: protocol, source IP address, source port, destination IP address and destination port. Two connections differing in any one of them are different connections; without the protocol it is called the 4-tuple.
example: (TCP, 198.51.100.7, 51000, 203.0.113.5, 443) and the same with source port 51001 are two separate connections.

definition: A socket in LISTEN that accepts connection attempts and produces separate sockets for accepted TCP connections. It is not the application data stream; Fast Open and implementation details can alter when an accept becomes available.
example: One listening socket on port 443 can produce hundreds of thousands of accepted sockets.

definition: The separate connected socket returned by accept(), leaving the listening socket available for further arrivals. In ordinary TCP, the pending handshake has completed before acceptance; Fast Open is a specified exception.
example: Every client of a web server gets its own accepted socket, all with local port 443.

definition: The socket call that attaches a socket to a local IP address and port number. Servers bind to a known port; clients usually skip it and let the kernel pick an ephemeral port.
example: s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9999)) makes the socket receive traffic sent to port 9999 on the loopback address.

definition: The standard name a computer uses for itself. It resolves to the loopback address (127.0.0.1 in IPv4, ::1 in IPv6), so traffic sent there goes through a virtual loopback interface and never leaves the machine.
example: A server bound to 127.0.0.1 can only be reached by programs on the same computer.

definition: A socket receive call that can also return the sender’s address. On an ordinary UDP socket it consumes at most one datagram, possibly truncating it when the supplied buffer is too small; stream-socket reads have different boundary rules.
example: data, addr = s.recvfrom(2048) returns up to 2,048 bytes of one datagram plus the sender's (IP, port).

definition: A socket send call that can supply a destination address with the data. On an ordinary unconnected UDP socket it sends one datagram, allowing the socket to address different peers; stream-socket semantics and limits differ.
example: s.sendto(data, addr) replies to whichever client addr names.

definition: A call associating a socket with a peer. An ordinary blocking TCP connect initiates establishment and waits for success or failure; a non-blocking call can remain in progress. UDP connect selects a default peer and receive filtering without a UDP handshake.
example: s.connect(("203.0.113.5", 443)) opens a TCP connection to port 443.

definition: The delay before something happens: for networks, how long data takes to get from one end to the other, or for a request to get its response. It is measured in time (milliseconds), unlike throughput, which is a rate.
example: A 100 ms round trip adds at least 100 ms of latency to every request that needs one.

definition: An outward exchange followed by a reply, whose elapsed time is a round-trip time. A conventional new TCP connection incurs a handshake exchange, but data in SYNs, Fast Open, reuse and the chosen measurement endpoints qualify timing claims.
example: A new ordinary TCP connection exchanges SYN, SYN+ACK and ACK before normal established operation.

definition: An exchange that establishes protocol state between endpoints. TCP exchanges and acknowledges sequence spaces; TLS establishes cryptographic parameters and can authenticate peers. Costs depend on version, retries, resumption and whether early data is used.
example: A conventional full TLS 1.3 handshake without retry adds one round trip after ordinary TCP setup.

definition: When one missing or slow item at the front of an ordered queue holds up everything behind it. In TCP, one lost segment stops later bytes reaching the application until it is retransmitted, even if they belong to unrelated requests.
example: On an HTTP/2 connection, a lost packet from a JavaScript file delays the CSS and images that arrived just after it.

definition: Extension Mechanisms for DNS: an addition to DNS that lets a client advertise that it can accept UDP responses larger than the original 512-byte limit, among other options.
example: A resolver using EDNS might advertise a 1,232-byte UDP buffer size.

definition: A bit in the DNS header meaning 'truncated': the full answer did not fit in the UDP response, so the client should ask again over TCP.
example: A large DNSSEC response over UDP may come back with TC set, prompting a TCP retry.

definition: A coordinated effort by DNS software vendors and operators to change defaults on an agreed date. The 2020 event recommended a 1,232-byte EDNS buffer size to avoid IP fragmentation.
example: After DNS Flag Day 2020, many resolvers default to a 1,232-byte UDP payload limit.

definition: Carrying DNS messages over a TCP connection instead of UDP, with a two-byte length before each message. It is used for large answers, zone transfers and when a UDP reply was truncated.
example: A resolver that receives a truncated UDP reply retries the same query as DNS over TCP.

definition: The unit of frequency: one event or cycle per second. An update rate of 60 Hz means 60 updates every second.
example: At 60 Hz, updates are about 16.7 ms apart.

definition: Real-time Transport Protocol: the standard format for carrying audio and video in calls and streaming, usually over UDP. It adds sequence numbers and timestamps so the receiver can play media in order and on time.
example: A video call might send RTP packets every 20 ms carrying compressed audio.

definition: Forward error correction: sending extra redundant data so the receiver can rebuild some lost or damaged data without asking for a retransmission. It suits real-time media, where waiting for a resend is too slow.
example: Sending one parity packet for every four media packets lets the receiver recover any single lost packet in the group.

definition: HTTP semantics carried over QUIC, specified by RFC 9114 in 2022. Independent QUIC streams avoid TCP connection-wide ordered-delivery gaps, while congestion control, flow control and application dependencies still create shared effects.
example: An HTTP/3 service can use QUIC over UDP port 443; that port is not mandatory for every QUIC service.

definition: The 2015 version of HTTP that multiplexes many requests and responses as separate streams over one TCP connection. Because TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, a single lost packet can delay every stream on the connection.
example: A page's CSS, JavaScript and images can all travel as HTTP/2 streams over one TCP connection.

definition: The HTTP version whose message syntax and framing are specified in RFC 9112. A connection can be persistent and support pipelined requests, with responses ordered; body length depends on method/status rules, transfer coding, Content-Length or closure.
example: A HEAD response can carry Content-Length metadata while containing no message body.

definition: Network Time Protocol: the protocol computers use to synchronise their clocks with time servers, usually over UDP port 123.
example: A server runs an NTP client so its clock stays within milliseconds of real time.

definition: Simple Network Management Protocol: a protocol for monitoring and managing network devices such as routers and switches, conventionally over UDP.
example: A monitoring system polls each switch over SNMP for its interface traffic counters.

definition: A standard for sending log messages from devices and programs to a log collector. The traditional transport is UDP port 514, though TCP and TLS transports also exist.
example: A firewall sends its logs to a central server using syslog.

definition: A modern, simple VPN protocol that encrypts IP packets and carries them inside UDP datagrams.
example: A WireGuard tunnel between two offices sends all traffic as encrypted UDP packets on one port.

definition: Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for logging in to and running commands on a remote machine, usually over TCP port 22.
example: ssh admin@server opens a remote terminal over an encrypted TCP connection.

definition: A widely used open-source relational database; its server listens on TCP port 3306 by default.
example: A web application connects to MySQL at db.internal:3306.

definition: An in-memory key-value cache often used in front of databases. Servers exposed to the internet with UDP enabled were abused in 2018 for huge amplification attacks.
example: Cloudflare reported Memcached reflection attacks reaching hundreds of gigabits per second in 2018.

definition: A denial-of-service attack in which the attacker sends small requests with the victim's address forged as the source, so open servers send much larger replies to the victim. UDP services with big responses and no handshake are the usual tools.
example: Queries of 100 Mbit/s with replies 50 times bigger send 5 Gbit/s at the victim.

definition: Forging a sender identity, most often a packet's source IP address. Replies to a spoofed address go to the forged address, which is how reflection attacks hit victims, and why UDP (with no handshake) cannot confirm who it is talking to.
example: An attacker spoofs a victim's address in DNS queries so all the answers flood the victim.

definition: How long a NAT retains an address/port translation mapping without qualifying traffic. RFC 4787 specifies that ordinary UDP mapping timers normally must not expire in less than two minutes, with a defined well-known-port exception; actual devices and application policies vary.
example: RFC 4787 normally requires a UDP mapping timer of at least two minutes; an application chooses keepalive timing for its actual path and requirements rather than assuming all devices meet that minimum.

definition: An IETF working document that can change, expire or be replaced and is not itself a standard. Some drafts become RFCs through the relevant stream process; RFCs can also be informational or experimental rather than standards.
example: BBRv3 was described in an IETF draft rather than an RFC.

definition: Where ordinary programs and libraries run, outside the operating-system kernel. Code there can be updated with the application, whereas kernel code changes with the operating system.
example: QUIC is usually implemented in user space, inside the browser or a server library.

definition: A set of open connections reused for multiple operations. Reuse can avoid repeated setup and reduce connection churn, but idle expiry, validation, resource limits and concurrency policy remain application concerns.
example: A web app keeps a pool of 20 database connections and lends one to each request.

definition: A continuous sequence of bytes with no built-in message boundaries, delivered in the order sent. TCP gives applications a byte stream, so two writes may arrive as one read, or one write as several reads.
example: Sending "hello" then "world" over TCP may be read as "helloworld" in one recv().

definition: The parts of TCP that open, maintain and close connections: the handshake, the state machine, graceful close with FINs and aborts with RST.
example: TIME_WAIT and SYN cookies are both connection-management mechanisms.

definition: In TCP, one unit of data: a TCP header plus a chunk of the byte stream, carried inside one IP packet; TCP chooses segment sizes itself, independent of how the application wrote the data. In LAN and security design the word also means a section of a network, such as an Ethernet segment or an isolated network segment.
example: A 4,000-byte write might leave as three segments of 1,460, 1,460 and 1,080 bytes.

definition: The control information at the start of every TCP segment: ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags, window, checksum and optional extras. It is 20 bytes without options and at most 60 bytes with them.
example: A pure ACK is just a TCP header with no data: 20 bytes, or 32 with the timestamp option.

definition: The TCP segment's first sequence-space position in that direction, held in a 32-bit header field. A SYN precedes any data in its segment and consumes one position, as does FIN; ordinary data consumes one position per byte.
example: A segment without SYN/FIN at sequence 1001 carrying 500 bytes ends at data byte 1500.

definition: The 32-bit TCP header field that tells the other side the next sequence number the receiver expects: in other words, every byte before it has arrived. It is only meaningful when the ACK flag is set.
example: ack=5001 means 'I have everything up to 5000; send 5001 next'.

definition: Single-bit fields in the TCP header that mark what a segment does: SYN opens, FIN closes, RST aborts, ACK says the acknowledgement number is valid, plus PSH, URG, ECE and CWR.
example: A handshake's second segment has both the SYN and ACK flags set: SYN+ACK.

definition: The second segment of the three-way handshake: the server's own SYN with the ACK flag set, acknowledging the client's SYN.
example: In reply to SYN seq=1000, a server sends SYN+ACK seq=5000 ack=1001.

definition: Acknowledgement: a TCP segment (or the flag in one) telling the sender which data has arrived. TCP ACKs are cumulative and carry the next sequence number the receiver expects.
example: After receiving bytes 1 to 1000, a receiver sends ACK 1001.

definition: The TCP flag meaning 'I have no more data to send'. Each direction of a connection is closed by its own FIN, which uses up one sequence number and must be acknowledged.
example: After sending bytes up to 1300, a client's FIN has seq=1301 and is acknowledged with ack=1302.

definition: The TCP reset flag, used to refuse or abort a connection when the segment passes the state-specific validation rules. A reset is not acknowledged as data; invalid resets can be ignored or challenged rather than immediately closing a connection.
example: A SYN to a port with no listener normally gets an RST back, which the client reports as 'connection refused'.

definition: The TCP push flag, associated with delivering data promptly rather than waiting indefinitely for a full buffer. It does not mark application message boundaries, and its relationship to writes depends on the implementation.
example: The last segment of an HTTP response usually has PSH set.

definition: The TCP 'urgent' flag, which marks some data as urgent using an urgent pointer. It is a legacy feature that new applications should not use.
example: Old Telnet used URG to send interrupt signals ahead of queued data.

definition: The 16-bit TCP header field in which a receiver advertises how many bytes, starting at its acknowledgement number, it is prepared to accept. Without window scaling it can say at most 65,535 bytes.
example: A window field of 65,535 with no scaling lets the sender have 64 KB unacknowledged.

definition: Optional extra fields after the fixed 20-byte TCP header, such as MSS, window scale, SACK and timestamps. All options together must fit in 40 bytes.
example: A typical SYN carries MSS, SACK-permitted, timestamp and window-scale options.

definition: The 4-bit TCP header field giving the header's length in 4-byte words, so the receiver knows where options end and data begins. Its largest value, 15, limits the header to 60 bytes.
example: A data offset of 5 means a 20-byte header with no options.

definition: Sender maximum segment size: the largest TCP data payload the sender can transmit in one segment, excluding TCP/IP headers. Congestion-control rules use it as a byte quantity; it depends on peer MSS and path/interface constraints.
example: RFC 5681 grows cwnd by about one SMSS per round trip in congestion avoidance.

definition: Receiver maximum segment size: the largest TCP data payload the receiver is willing to accept, excluding headers. Classic delayed-ACK guidance recommends an ACK at least for every second full-sized segment or every two RMSS bytes of new data.
example: With an RMSS of 1,460 bytes, a receiver should ACK at least every 2,920 bytes of new data.

definition: Initial sequence number: the starting sequence number each side picks for its direction of a new TCP connection and sends in its SYN. It is chosen to be hard to guess, to reject stale segments and resist spoofing.
example: A client with ISN 1000 numbers its first data byte 1001, because the SYN uses 1000.

definition: A copy of a segment from earlier, delayed in the network, that arrives after it is no longer wanted. If it fell inside a new connection's sequence space it could be accepted as data, which random ISNs and TIME_WAIT guard against.
example: A SYN from a connection attempt minutes ago that finally arrives at a server is an old duplicate.

definition: An attacker who cannot see the traffic between two hosts but can send forged packets towards them, so must guess values such as sequence numbers.
example: An off-path attacker trying to inject an RST must guess the exact sequence number.

definition: One particular use of a 5-tuple: a later connection with the same addresses and ports is a new incarnation. TCP tries to keep segments from an old incarnation out of a new one.
example: Reconnecting from the same source port to the same server creates a new incarnation of that 5-tuple.

definition: Linux's small record for a half-open TCP connection: what it keeps after receiving a SYN and sending SYN+ACK, while it waits for the final ACK.
example: During a SYN flood the listener's request sockets fill up with attempts that will never complete.

definition: In this module, a pending handshake whose server SYN+ACK has not yet received its final acknowledgement. RFC 9293 also uses half-open for a connection where one peer has lost or closed state without the other knowing; SYN cookies can avoid ordinary per-attempt pending state.
example: A server under a SYN flood has thousands of half-open connections that never complete.

definition: A denial-of-service attack that sends many SYNs, often from spoofed addresses, so the server fills its queue of half-open connections and starts dropping real clients' SYNs.
example: An attacker sending 100,000 spoofed SYNs a second can fill a listener's SYN queue in moments.

definition: The kernel's list of half-open connections on a listening socket: SYNs that have been answered with SYN+ACK but not yet completed by the client's ACK.
example: When the SYN queue overflows, Linux can switch to SYN cookies.

definition: A defence against SYN floods: instead of storing state for a half-open connection, the server encodes what it needs into its SYN+ACK sequence number using a secret. A genuine client's ACK returns that number plus one, so the server can check and rebuild the connection.
example: Linux's tcp_syncookies = 1 sends SYN cookies only when the SYN queue overflows.

definition: Able to carry data in both directions at the same time, independently. A TCP connection is full duplex, so each direction is opened and closed on its own.
example: A server can keep sending a response after the client has closed its sending direction.

definition: Closing TCP sending directions with FIN and acknowledgement rather than an abortive reset. An ordinary sequential exchange can use four segments, or combine an ACK and FIN; retransmissions and simultaneous closure can change the count. Transport acknowledgement does not prove application processing.
example: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK is a common teaching trace, without asserting a retransmission-free count for all closes.

definition: Closing only your sending direction of a TCP connection with a FIN while still receiving. The peer sees end of stream but can keep sending its reply.
example: A client calls shutdown(SHUT_WR) after its request, then reads the whole response.

definition: A socket call that closes one or both directions of a connection without releasing the socket. SHUT_WR sends a FIN (no more data from me) but keeps the receiving direction open.
example: sock.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR) tells the server the request is complete.

definition: The endpoint that initiates an ordinary sequential TCP graceful close, while the other is called the passive closer. In that sequence the active closer enters TIME_WAIT; simultaneous close, resets and exceptional reuse paths need separate rules.
example: If a web server closes first after its response, the server is the active closer and holds TIME_WAIT.

definition: A TCP closing state retained to handle repeated FINs and protect against old segments from a prior connection incarnation. The specified ordinary interval is twice the assumed maximum segment lifetime; Linux v6.12 uses a 60-second interval, with reuse and event-handling qualifications.
example: A proxy closing 600 connections a second holds about 36,000 TIME_WAIT entries at once.

definition: Maximum segment lifetime: the longest a TCP segment is assumed to survive in the network before being discarded. RFC 793 suggested 2 minutes; TIME_WAIT lasts twice the MSL.
example: With an MSL of 2 minutes, TIME_WAIT would last 4 minutes; Linux instead uses 60 s.

definition: The set of 11 states a TCP connection moves through (such as LISTEN, ESTABLISHED and TIME_WAIT) and the events that move it between them, defined in RFC 9293.
example: A client goes CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED as it opens a connection.

definition: The TCP state meaning no connection exists. Every connection starts and ends here.
example: A socket returns to CLOSED after LAST_ACK receives its final acknowledgement.

definition: The TCP state of a server socket waiting for incoming connection attempts, entered when the program calls listen().
example: A web server's socket on port 443 sits in LISTEN.

definition: A TCP state waiting for a matching connection request after sending an active-open SYN. An ordinary client expects SYN+ACK, but simultaneous open can first receive a SYN and enter SYN-RECEIVED.
example: connect() puts a socket in SYN_SENT until the server answers.

definition: A TCP state waiting for acknowledgement after both receiving and sending a connection request. It commonly follows a server SYN+ACK but can also arise from simultaneous active opens.
example: During a SYN flood, many attempts sit in SYN_RCVD until they time out.

definition: The normal TCP state of an open connection, in which data flows in both directions.
example: After the three-way handshake both ends are ESTABLISHED.

definition: The TCP state of the active closer just after it sends its FIN, waiting for that FIN to be acknowledged (or for the peer's FIN).
example: close() on an established socket moves it to FIN_WAIT_1.

definition: The TCP state of the active closer after its FIN has been acknowledged, waiting for the peer's FIN. The peer may still send data meanwhile.
example: A client in FIN_WAIT_2 can still be receiving the server's response.

definition: A TCP state entered after an acceptable peer FIN when the local sending direction has not yet closed. It can be legitimate while finishing a response; persistent unexplained accumulation calls for handler and descriptor investigation rather than proving a leak by itself.
example: A server leaking sockets on an error path accumulates thousands in CLOSE_WAIT.

definition: The TCP state of the passive closer after sending its own FIN, waiting for the final acknowledgement before going to CLOSED.
example: After first receiving and acknowledging a peer FIN, an endpoint sends its own FIN and waits in LAST_ACK for its acknowledgement.

definition: The TCP state reached during a simultaneous close: both sides sent FIN, and this side has received the peer's FIN before its own FIN was acknowledged.
example: Two peers whose FINs cross in the network both pass through CLOSING on the way to TIME_WAIT.

definition: Both TCP endpoints initiate graceful close without first receiving the other FIN. When crossing FINs are processed before acknowledgement of each endpoint's own FIN, both pass through CLOSING and later TIME_WAIT; combined ACK/FIN event ordering can give a different intermediate transition.
example: Two crossing FINs that do not acknowledge each other can put both endpoints through CLOSING.

definition: A Linux setting enabling reuse of TIME_WAIT sockets for new connections when implementation protocol checks permit it. Retrieved documentation lists default 2 for loopback only and a reuse-delay setting; enabling it is not a universal solution for tuple exhaustion.
example: Setting tcp_tw_reuse = 1 can ease ephemeral port exhaustion on a busy proxy.

definition: A former Linux setting that sped up TIME_WAIT expiry using timestamps but broke clients behind NAT, whose timestamps differ. It was removed in Linux 4.12.
example: Old tuning guides recommending tcp_tw_recycle are outdated: the option no longer exists.

definition: A Linux command-line tool (socket statistics) that lists sockets and their TCP state, with -i adding internal details such as cwnd, RTT and retransmissions.
example: ss -ti shows each connection's congestion window and smoothed RTT.

definition: The error a client gets when its connection attempt is answered with RST, usually because nothing is listening on that port. A silently dropped SYN gives a timeout instead.
example: Connecting to a closed port on a reachable host fails quickly with ECONNREFUSED.

definition: A socket option controlling close behaviour for pending output. On Linux TCP, enabling linger with a zero timeout requests an abortive close rather than the ordinary graceful FIN exchange; descriptor references and connection state still matter.
example: A load balancer may set SO_LINGER to 0 so its closes send RST and avoid TIME_WAIT.

definition: Ending a TCP connection without the normal acknowledged FIN exchange, generally by reset. Unread/unsent application data can be lost; the result and treatment of pre-existing closing state depend on platform and connection state.
example: Closing a socket with SO_LINGER set to 0 performs an abortive close.

definition: An ACK sent under TCP robustness rules in response to specified suspicious segments. RFC 5961 challenges a reset whose sequence number is in the window but is not exactly the next expected position; this reduces blind guessing opportunities without cryptographically authenticating the peer.
example: An in-window but inexact reset receives a challenge ACK under the specified RFC 5961 rule.

definition: In TCP's specification, the next sequence number the receiver expects: the value it sends as its acknowledgement number.
example: If RCV.NXT is 5001, bytes up to 5000 have arrived in order.

definition: The Linux interface and command for reading and changing kernel settings at run time, such as net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control.
example: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies prints the current SYN-cookie mode.

definition: Keeping an HTTP connection open after a response so later requests reuse it, avoiding new TCP and TLS handshakes. It is about connection reuse, unlike TCP keepalive probes.
example: With keep-alive, a page's ten requests can share one connection instead of opening ten.

definition: Sending another operation over a connection that is still usable, avoiding fresh setup and reducing close/reconnect churn. Idle time, congestion-state restart, protocol limits and peer closure can change the benefit.
example: In an ideal fresh TCP plus full TLS 1.3 example, setup and one request/response take three RTTs; an already usable connection can reduce that example to one RTT.

definition: Sending the same bytes in differently sized segments than before, for example combining two lost segments into one retransmission. TCP can do this because it numbers bytes, not packets.
example: Two lost 500-byte segments can be retransmitted as one 1,000-byte segment.

definition: When a 32-bit sequence number passes its largest value and starts again from 0. At high speeds this can happen within seconds, so an old segment could carry a number that looks current.
example: At 10 Gbit/s the sequence space wraps about every 3.4 seconds.

definition: Gibibyte: 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes, the binary counterpart of the gigabyte. The 32-bit sequence space covers 4 GiB.

A negotiated TCP option carrying a timestamp value and an echo selected under protocol rules. It supports RTT measurement and PAWS; the option is ten bytes and commonly occupies twelve bytes with alignment padding, without always echoing the latest-arriving segment.
example: With timestamps, a sender can measure RTT even from a retransmitted segment's ACK.

definition: Protection Against Wrapped Sequences: a TCP mechanism that uses the timestamp option to reject old segments whose sequence numbers have come round again after wraparound.
example: On a 40 Gbit/s link, where sequence numbers wrap in under a second, PAWS stops a stale segment being accepted as new data.

definition: Rules for comparing numbers that wrap round, such as 32-bit sequence numbers and timestamps: a value counts as 'later' if it is less than half the number space ahead. This keeps comparisons working after wraparound.
example: With 32-bit serial arithmetic, 5 counts as later than 4,294,967,290 because it is only 11 steps ahead.

definition: An acknowledgement that confirms every byte before a given number in one go. TCP ACKs are cumulative, so one later ACK covers several earlier lost ACKs, but it cannot say anything about data received beyond a gap.
example: ACK 5001 confirms bytes 1 to 5000 all arrived.

definition: An ACK that repeats a cumulative acknowledgement and satisfies additional algorithm-specific conditions. Out-of-order arrivals can produce duplicate ACKs, but repeated numbers alone do not uniquely establish packet loss; classic RFC 5681 fast retransmit requires three qualifying duplicates.
example: If segment 1001 is lost, segments 2001, 3001 and 4001 each produce a duplicate ACK 1001.

definition: A simple recovery scheme that, after a loss, resends the missing packet and everything sent after it, even data that arrived safely.
example: If segment 1001 of five is lost, Go-Back-N resends 1001, 2001, 3001 and 4001.

definition: Selective acknowledgement: a TCP option in which the receiver lists blocks of data it holds beyond the cumulative ACK point, so the sender can resend only what is missing. It is enabled by SACK-permitted options in the SYNs.
example: ACK 1001 SACK 2001-5001 says 'I'm missing 1001 to 2000 but have 2001 to 5000'.

definition: Duplicate SACK: an extension where the receiver uses the first SACK block to report data it received twice. It helps the sender spot retransmissions that were not needed.
example: A SACK block 8001-9001 below the cumulative ACK 9001 is a D-SACK report of a duplicate.

definition: When a receiver discards data it had already reported with SACK, for example under memory pressure. Because it is allowed, a sender cannot treat SACKed data as safely delivered until it is cumulatively acknowledged.
example: A receiver short of memory may renege on SACKed bytes, so the sender keeps them buffered.

definition: Resending data that was not actually lost, only delayed or reordered. It wastes bandwidth and can make congestion control slow down for no reason.
example: If a segment is merely late and the sender resends it, the receiver gets it twice: a spurious retransmission.

definition: Retransmission timeout, used by TCP's retransmission timer. RFC 6298 adds the larger of clock granularity and four RTT variations to the smoothed RTT, then applies timer bounds and policy; expiry retransmits the earliest unacknowledged segment and backs the timer off.
example: With SRTT 100 ms and RTTVAR 50 ms, the RTO is 300 ms (before any minimum is applied).

definition: Smoothed round-trip time: TCP's running average of measured RTTs. Each new sample moves it one eighth of the way towards the sample.
example: With SRTT 100 ms, a new 120 ms sample gives SRTT 102.5 ms.

definition: TCP's smoothed estimate of the absolute deviation of RTT samples from the prior smoothed RTT. It is a time quantity, not statistical variance measured in squared time; RFC 6298 uses it to provide the retransmission margin.
example: With SRTT 100 ms, RTTVAR 50 ms and a 120 ms sample, RTTVAR becomes 42.5 ms.

definition: A running average updated by keeping most of the old value and blending in a fixed share of each new sample, so older samples fade away gradually.
example: With weight 1/8, an average of 100 and a new sample of 120 becomes 0.875 × 100 + 0.125 × 120 = 102.5.

definition: The smallest step a system's timer can measure or schedule, its 'tick'. The RTO formula uses it as a floor for the safety margin.
example: A kernel timer with 1 ms granularity cannot schedule a 0.3 ms timeout.

definition: Doubling the wait after each failed attempt. TCP doubles its RTO each time the timer fires for the same data, so a broken path is not hammered with retransmissions.
example: With a 300 ms RTO, retransmissions go out after 0.3, 0.9, 2.1 and 4.5 seconds.

definition: The rule excluding ambiguous RTT samples from retransmitted data: an ACK might cover the original or its retransmission. A valid mechanism such as negotiated timestamp echo processing can disambiguate a sample; its selection rules still matter.
example: An ACK arriving 50 ms after a retransmission and 350 ms after the original gives no usable sample.

definition: A Linux setting for how many times TCP retransmits unacknowledged data before giving up on the connection. Its default of 15 corresponds, under Linux's documented model, to a timeout of at least 924.6 seconds.
example: Lowering tcp_retries2 makes connections to vanished peers fail sooner.

definition: Resending a segment as soon as three duplicate ACKs suggest it was lost, instead of waiting for the retransmission timer.
example: After the third duplicate ACK 1001, the sender resends 1001 at once.

definition: The congestion-control phase that follows fast retransmit: the sender cuts its window (Reno roughly halves it) but keeps sending, using the stream of duplicate ACKs as a signal that packets are still getting through, rather than restarting from one segment.
example: Reno enters fast recovery after three duplicate ACKs and leaves it when the lost data is acknowledged.

definition: A TCP rule that lets a sender transmit new data on the first two duplicate ACKs, so a small window still generates enough later arrivals to trigger fast retransmit.
example: With four segments in flight and one lost, Limited Transmit sends extra data so three duplicate ACKs can arrive.

definition: Loss of the last segment or segments of a transfer. Nothing follows them to produce duplicate ACKs, so classic fast retransmit cannot fire and only a timer (RTO or TLP) recovers them.
example: If the final segment of an API response is lost, the sender sees no duplicate ACKs at all.

definition: Recent ACKnowledgement, a TCP loss detector using delivery of later-transmitted data, transmit times, an RTT estimate and reordering tolerance. Its deadline is not universally a fixed quarter RTT after a SACK arrives; adaptation and per-transmission age matter.
example: Delivery of a later-sent segment can supply evidence used with an earlier transmission's age and the reordering allowance.

definition: The RFC 8985 combination of time-based RACK loss detection and eligible Tail Loss Probes. It can reduce reliance on long retransmission timeouts, but recovery time depends on flight contents, timer rules, ACK arrivals and subsequent loss.
example: A delivered probe and its ACK can reveal tail loss before the retransmission timeout.

definition: Tail Loss Probe, a permitted TCP probe intended to elicit delivery feedback when later data is unavailable. Its baseline timeout is twice SRTT, adjusted for a single outstanding segment and capped by the RTO deadline; eligibility and new-data/retransmission selection rules apply.
example: With SRTT 40 ms, TLP fires about 80 ms after the last transmission.

definition: Probe timeout: how long TCP's Tail Loss Probe waits before sending a probe, with a baseline of twice the smoothed RTT plus adjustments. QUIC also has a probe timeout, computed by its own formula.
example: With SRTT 40 ms the baseline PTO is 80 ms.

definition: A Linux tool that prints the kernel's network counters, such as TcpRetransSegs (segments retransmitted) and TcpExtListenOverflows.
example: nstat -az TcpRetransSegs shows how many segments the host has retransmitted.

definition: The network researcher whose 1988 paper 'Congestion Avoidance and Control' introduced TCP's RTT estimator, slow start and congestion avoidance after the 1986 congestion collapses.
example: Jacobson's approach, a smoothed RTT average plus a multiple of its mean deviation, is still the basis of the RTO rules in RFC 6298.

definition: Stopping a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. In TCP the receiver advertises a receive window saying how much more data it will accept, and the sender stays within it.
example: A phone reading slowly advertises a small window, so the server sends no faster than the phone reads.

definition: The receive window: an advertisement of acceptable TCP sequence space from the acknowledgement point. It reflects receiver capacity and update policy rather than exact free socket memory; window shrinkage, earlier in-flight data and probes require additional rules.
example: An advertised 65,535-byte window identifies acceptable sequence space, not exactly 65,535 bytes of unused socket memory.

definition: The sender's own limit on unacknowledged data, set by its congestion-control algorithm to avoid overloading the network. It is never sent in a header; the sender uses whichever of cwnd and the receive window is smaller.
example: A cwnd of 40 segments of 1,460 bytes lets 58,400 bytes be in flight.

definition: Data that has been sent but not yet acknowledged. RFC 5681 calls the amount FlightSize; congestion and flow control both limit it.
example: With 30,000 bytes in flight and a 58,400-byte window, 28,400 more bytes may be sent.

definition: Kernel memory where a socket holds arriving data until the application reads it. When it fills because the application is not reading, the advertised window shrinks towards zero.
example: If a program stops calling recv(), its receive buffer fills and the sender is told to stop.

definition: Socket memory retaining data accepted from an application while transport sending or acknowledgement is pending. A successful send reports local acceptance of some bytes, not their remote receipt or processing; copying, zero-copy facilities and accounting depend on the API.
example: For an ordinary copied socket send, a returned byte count reports local acceptance into transport buffering; it does not say when the peer receives or processes those bytes.

definition: A range of sequence numbers the sender may have outstanding; it slides forward as ACKs arrive. Bytes left of the window are acknowledged, bytes inside are in flight or sendable, and bytes to the right must wait.
example: When an ACK for 1,000 bytes arrives, the window's left edge moves forward by 1,000.

definition: In TCP's specification, the oldest unacknowledged sequence number: the left edge of the sender's window.
example: If bytes up to 1000 are acknowledged, SND.UNA is 1001.

definition: In TCP's specification, the next sequence number the sender will use for new data.
example: After sending bytes 1001 to 3000, SND.NXT is 3001.

definition: Bandwidth-delay product: link capacity multiplied by round-trip time, the amount of data that must be in flight to keep the path fully busy. A window smaller than the BDP leaves the link partly idle.
example: 1 Gbit/s × 100 ms = 100 Mbit = 12.5 MB.

definition: A TCP SYN option selecting a shift count from zero to fourteen for that endpoint's later receive-window advertisements. Both peers must send the option for scaling to operate; SYN and SYN+ACK window fields themselves are unscaled.
example: With shift count 7, a window field of 1,000 means 128,000 bytes.

definition: Automatic adjustment of TCP socket-buffer capacity under operating-system policy and configured limits. On Linux, explicitly setting SO_RCVBUF disables receive autotuning for that socket; buffer memory is not identical to advertised payload window.
example: On a long-distance download, autotuning can grow the receive buffer from 128 KiB to several megabytes.

definition: Linux settings giving three values (minimum, default, maximum) for TCP receive (rmem) and send (wmem) buffer sizes; autotuning works within them.
example: The kernel documentation lists a 131,072-byte default for tcp_rmem.

definition: A socket option that sets the receive buffer size. On Linux it doubles the requested value for bookkeeping and switches off receive autotuning for that socket.
example: Setting SO_RCVBUF to 64 KB on a long-distance link can cap throughput at a few Mbit/s.

definition: A socket option that sets the send buffer size, the amount of unsent and unacknowledged data the kernel will hold for the socket.
example: Raising SO_SNDBUF does not help if Nagle, not buffer space, is holding data back.

definition: The socket call that sets an option on a socket, such as TCP_NODELAY or SO_REUSEADDR; getsockopt() reads one back.
example: s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_NODELAY, 1) disables Nagle.

definition: A TCP receive-window advertisement of zero, stopping ordinary new-data transmission into that window. Allowed probes can solicit updates; a capture shows receiver-side restriction but does not alone establish why it occurred.
example: A server blocked on disk I/O stops reading its socket and advertises a zero window.

definition: A segment, usually a pure ACK, sent by a receiver to advertise a larger window after its application has read data.
example: After the application reads 64 KB, the receiver sends a window update reopening the window.

definition: A TCP segment that carries an acknowledgement (and window) but no data. Because it uses no sequence numbers, TCP never retransmits it if it is lost.
example: A window update is normally a pure ACK.

definition: A mechanism scheduling probes when queued data meets a zero receive window. A successfully delivered probe/reply exchange can reveal an update that was lost; backoff limits traffic, while continued loss or endpoint failure can still prevent progress.
example: If a probe and reply are delivered after a lost window update, the sender can learn that the window reopened.

definition: A permitted sender probe used while a receiver advertises zero window, eliciting a reply with the current window. A delivered probe/reply can reveal reopened space; probe construction and backoff follow protocol/implementation rules and cannot guarantee progress through continued loss.
example: After a lost window update, a later successful probe exchange can allow sending to resume.

definition: A failure mode where the receiver advertises tiny windows and the sender fills each at once, so the connection sends many segments carrying only a few bytes each, wasting most of the bandwidth on headers.
example: Segments of 10 bytes with 40 bytes of headers use only 20 % of each packet for data.

definition: The receiver-side fix for silly window syndrome: do not advertise more space until it has grown by at least one MSS or half the buffer, whichever is smaller.
example: With a 1,460-byte MSS and a 64 KiB buffer, the receiver waits until 1,460 bytes are free.

definition: A sender rule from 1984: while data is unacknowledged, hold back small writes until either an ACK arrives or a full segment's worth is ready, then send them together. It cuts tiny packets but can delay request/response traffic.
example: Keystrokes typed during one RTT leave as one packet instead of many 41-byte ones.

definition: An old, unencrypted protocol for logging in to a remote computer's terminal over TCP. Each keystroke could be sent as its own packet, the problem Nagle's algorithm addressed.
example: Telnet has been replaced by SSH, which encrypts the session.

definition: A receiver optimisation: wait briefly before acknowledging, hoping to combine the ACK with response data or cover two segments with one ACK. RFC 9293 requires the delay to be under 500 ms.
example: A receiver might hold an ACK for up to 40 ms waiting for the application's reply.

definition: Sending an acknowledgement inside a segment that also carries data going the other way, instead of in a separate ACK segment.
example: A server's HTTP response segment also acknowledges the request: the ACK is piggybacked.

definition: The pattern of an application making two small writes and then waiting to read a reply. With Nagle on the sender and delayed ACK on the receiver it can stall until the delayed-ACK timer fires.
example: Sending a header and body in separate send() calls, then waiting for the response, is write-write-read.

definition: A TCP socket option disabling Nagle's small-new-data waiting condition. Other buffering, flow/congestion windows, pacing and packetisation rules still apply, so it does not guarantee immediate transmission or one packet per write.
example: Go documents NoDelay enabled by default for its TCPConn API; other APIs require their own checks.

definition: A Linux socket option that holds back partial segments while the application assembles data from several writes, then sends full segments; there is a timeout ceiling on the hold.
example: A web server corks the socket, writes headers, sends a file, then uncorks.

definition: A Linux send flag indicating that more data follows. For TCP it supplies a per-call effect similar to TCP_CORK, helping coalesce data without guaranteeing that the pieces form exactly one packet.
example: send(header, MSG_MORE) followed by send(body) lets both leave in one segment.

definition: A Linux socket option that makes the receiver send ACKs immediately instead of delaying them. It is not permanent: the kernel can return to delayed-ACK mode later.
example: Setting TCP_QUICKACK after each read can reduce delayed-ACK stalls, but needs measuring.

definition: Socket calls that send several separate buffers in one call (scatter/gather I/O), so a header and body can be handed to TCP together without first copying them into one buffer. They can still send only part of the data.
example: sock.sendmsg([header, body]) supplies both pieces at once.

definition: A state where a network is busy but delivers almost nothing useful, because senders keep retransmitting into overloaded queues and most of the traffic is copies that will be dropped. It happened on the early Internet in 1986.
example: In October 1986 one Berkeley link fell from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s, a factor of 800.

definition: The sender-side rules that decide how fast to send so the network is not overloaded: grow the sending window while things look fine, and cut it when loss, delay or ECN marks signal congestion.
example: Reno, CUBIC and BBR are three congestion-control algorithms.

definition: Evidence a sender treats as meaning the network is overloaded, such as a lost packet, a rising RTT or an ECN mark. Each congestion-control algorithm chooses which signals it reacts to.
example: Reno's congestion signals are duplicate ACKs and timeouts; DCTCP's is the fraction of ECN-marked packets.

definition: The congestion window a new connection starts with, before any ACKs. RFC 6928 allows up to about ten segments (IW10, 14,600 bytes with a 1,460-byte MSS).
example: With IW10, a server can send ten full segments in its first flight.

definition: A congestion-control phase that increases the sender window as new data is acknowledged. Under an ideal full-flight, ACK-per-segment model it doubles each RTT; delayed ACKs, byte counting, thresholds and other limits can change the growth.
example: Starting at 10 segments, slow start reaches 80 segments after three round trips.

definition: Slow start threshold: a window threshold used to choose between slow start and congestion avoidance. RFC 5681 reduces it using a ceiling based on half FlightSize with a two-segment floor; actual algorithm/version policy and repeated-timeout rules matter.
example: With 40 segments in flight at a loss, Reno sets ssthresh to 20.

definition: A congestion-control phase probing for capacity after slow start. Classic Reno grows by approximately one full-sized segment per RTT under suitable ACK and traffic assumptions; other algorithms such as CUBIC use different growth rules.
example: In congestion avoidance a 40-segment window becomes 41 after one loss-free round trip.

definition: Growing the congestion window by a fixed amount (one segment for Reno) each round trip without congestion.
example: Additive increase takes cwnd from 20 to 30 segments in ten round trips.

definition: Cutting the congestion window to a fixed fraction of its size when congestion is signalled: 0.5 for Reno, 0.7 for CUBIC.
example: Reno's multiplicative decrease takes a 40-segment window to 20.

definition: Additive increase, multiplicative decrease: grow linearly while things are fine and cut by a fraction on congestion. Chiu and Jain showed that, in a simplified model, this drives competing flows towards equal shares.
example: Two flows at 30 and 10 segments both add 1 per RTT; halving takes 15 from one and 5 from the other, narrowing the gap.

definition: Classic TCP congestion control combining slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. RFC 5681 thresholds use FlightSize; temporary recovery inflation and timeout loss-window rules mean it is more detailed than halving cwnd on every loss.
example: In the ideal congestion-avoidance model, Reno grows by about one segment per RTT and roughly halves its full-flight window on a qualifying fast-recovery event; timeouts differ.

definition: The earlier TCP congestion-control variant (1988) that reset the congestion window to one segment on every loss. Reno improved on it with fast recovery.
example: After three duplicate ACKs Tahoe restarts from one segment, while Reno only halves its window.

definition: A refinement of Reno's fast recovery (RFC 6582) that handles several losses in one window without leaving recovery after the first repair.
example: When two segments in one window are lost, NewReno repairs both in one recovery episode.

definition: The congestion window TCP uses right after a retransmission timeout: at most one full-sized segment, after which slow start begins again.
example: After an RTO, a 40-segment cwnd collapses to the one-segment loss window.

definition: The repeated rise and fall of a congestion window. In the ideal Reno congestion-avoidance illustration, linear growth alternates with halving on a qualifying loss event; timeouts, different algorithms and unequal cycles change that shape.
example: A window climbing from 20 to 40 and halving back to 20 draws one tooth of the sawtooth.

definition: The way TCP's sending is paced by arriving ACKs: each ACK signals data has left the network, letting the sender release new data at roughly the rate the path delivers it.
example: Under a one-full-segment-per-ACK teaching model with open windows and ready data, an ACK every millisecond can permit a segment every millisecond; ACKs need not correspond one-to-one to segments.

definition: A congestion-window update based on newly acknowledged bytes rather than ACK count alone. RFC 3465 specifies appropriate-byte-counting variants with bounds on per-ACK growth; one ACK for two segments does not universally require two-segment growth.
example: RFC 3465 discusses bounded per-ACK window growth using the newly acknowledged byte count.

definition: A congestion controller specified in RFC 9438 using an elapsed-time cubic window target and a Reno-friendly estimate. Its normal congestion-event reduction retains 70%; recovery, timeout, fast-convergence and application-limited handling qualify the pure curve.
example: The isolated cubic epoch with previous maximum 100 segments regains that target at about 4.2 seconds; this is not a universal transfer timing.

definition: CUBIC's comparison with a Reno-like window estimate, allowing that estimate to govern when it exceeds the cubic target. This improves coexistence and low-delay behaviour without guaranteeing equal rates or that an actual CUBIC flow always outperforms an actual Reno flow.
example: The Reno-friendly estimate can dominate the pure cubic target on a short-RTT path.

definition: A CUBIC heuristic: if a loss happens below the previous maximum, assume a new flow has arrived and lower the remembered maximum further, freeing bandwidth for the newcomer sooner.
example: With fast convergence, a loss at 90 segments after a previous peak of 100 sets the new target maximum below 90.

definition: A sending period constrained by available application data rather than by the transport’s current sending allowance. Congestion-control algorithms have specific rules for such periods; CUBIC excludes application-limited time from its cubic epoch and BBRv1 guards against misleading low delivery-rate samples.
example: An application producing 2 Mbit/s while the transport can currently send faster is application-limited; a 100 Mbit/s link alone would not establish that allowance.

definition: Congestion control that uses packet loss as a congestion signal, as Reno and CUBIC do; ECN can signal the response before a drop. A saturated flow with a large unmanaged tail-drop queue can build a standing backlog, but queue growth depends on AQM, feedback and other limits.
example: A continuously backlogged CUBIC flow can build a standing queue at a tail-drop bottleneck; ECN/AQM and sender limits can change the outcome.

definition: Packet loss caused by effects such as transmission corruption rather than an overflowing congestion queue. A policer can also drop packets due to a rate policy, which is distinct from independent random corruption; loss-based senders can reduce their windows in either case.
example: Random link corruption can cause repeated window reductions even when a congestion queue is empty.

definition: A traffic-conditioning function enforcing a profile, for example with token-bucket state. It can drop or remark non-conforming packets rather than delaying them; burst allowances mean it need not drop every packet above an instantaneous nominal rate.
example: A 100 Mbit/s token-bucket policy can permit a configured burst before treating additional traffic as non-conforming.

definition: Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time: a family of model-based congestion-control algorithms estimating delivery capacity and baseline RTT to control pacing and in-flight data. BBRv1, v2 and v3 differ in details, including loss response and coexistence; this module gives versioned v1 examples.
example: On a 100 Mbit/s path with a 20 ms base RTT, BBR aims to keep about 250 KB in flight.

definition: BBR's estimate of bottleneck delivery capacity. Linux v6.12 BBRv1 uses a windowed maximum of delivery-rate samples over ten packet-timed rounds, with application-limited safeguards; it need not equal a link's advertised physical rate.
example: An example estimated delivery capacity of 100 Mbit/s is 12,500,000 payload bytes per second.

definition: BBR's baseline RTT estimate. Linux v6.12 BBRv1 uses a ten-second windowed minimum with ProbeRTT refresh rules; endpoint and serialization costs or persistent queues can remain, so this is not pure physical propagation delay.
example: If RTT samples range from 20 to 80 ms as queues come and go, RTprop is about 20 ms.

definition: Spreading a sender's packets evenly over time at a chosen rate instead of sending a whole window in one burst. It reduces queue spikes and is central to BBR.
example: Pacing 10 packets over a 10 ms RTT sends one every millisecond instead of all ten at once.

definition: A multiplier applied to BBR's estimated bandwidth to form a target pacing rate. Values above one can probe and values below one can drain; phase values and transition rules are version-specific.
example: Linux v6.12 BBRv1 uses a 1.25 phase in its ProbeBW gain cycle.

definition: A BBR steady probing phase. Linux v6.12 BBRv1 cycles pacing gains through 1.25, 0.75 and six 1.0 phases, with timing and in-flight transition conditions; later BBR versions use different rules.
example: The v6.12 BBRv1 gain cycle includes one 1.25 phase, one 0.75 phase and six 1.0 phases.

definition: A BBR phase refreshing a baseline RTT estimate. In Linux v6.12 BBRv1, qualifying minimum-RTT expiry reduces toward four packets and requires at least 200 ms plus a completed round; application idleness and state conditions affect whether and when it runs.
example: A qualifying v6.12 BBRv1 ProbeRTT phase requires the minimum duration and a completed packet-timed round.

definition: Linux's 'Fair Queue' packet scheduler, which keeps per-flow queues and can enforce each socket's pacing rate. Linux BBR can use it or pace internally.
example: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root fq installs the fq scheduler.

definition: Congestion Experienced: the ECN codepoint a router sets in a packet's IP header to say 'I am congested', instead of dropping it.
example: A CE-marked packet is still delivered; only its congestion signal is echoed back.

definition: ECN-Echo: the TCP flag a receiver sets in its ACKs to tell the sender a CE-marked packet arrived. It keeps setting it until the sender confirms with CWR.
example: After receiving one CE-marked packet, a receiver sets ECE on its ACKs.

definition: Congestion Window Reduced, a TCP control bit used in classic RFC 3168 ECN feedback to acknowledge the sender's congestion response. The numerical reduction follows the applicable algorithm; later feedback schemes reuse control bits differently.
example: Classic ECN uses CWR after responding to ECE; the chosen congestion controller determines the numerical adjustment.

definition: The two-bit ECN field in the IP header: values mark a packet as not ECN-capable, ECN-capable (ECT), or Congestion Experienced (CE).
example: A sender using ECN sends packets with an ECT codepoint so routers may mark rather than drop them.

definition: Data Center TCP, an ECN-based congestion controller from RFC 8257. It smooths the fraction of marked data bytes and scales a window reduction accordingly, aiming for low queues in a suitably configured data-centre environment; outcomes depend on deployment.
example: A stable marking estimate of 0.1 corresponds to retaining about 95% in the simplified reduction.

definition: A deprecated ICMP congestion message. RFC 6633 requires hosts to discard it silently and prohibits routers from originating it; it is distinct from ECN’s in-band packet marking and feedback.
example: Modern hosts ignore ICMP Source Quench messages.

definition: On Linux, the socket option (TCP_CONGESTION) and system setting (tcp_congestion_control) that choose the congestion-control algorithm, such as cubic or bbr.
example: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = bbr makes BBR the default for new connections.

definition: Dah-Ming Chiu and Raj Jain, whose 1989 paper showed that additive increase with multiplicative decrease drives competing flows towards a fair, efficient share in a simplified feedback model.
example: Chiu and Jain's diagrams show two flows' rates zig-zagging towards the equal-share line.

definition: The time it takes to put a packet's bits onto a link: its size divided by the link rate. It matters on slow links and for large transfers.
example: 10,000 bytes at 10 Mbit/s take 80,000 / 10,000,000 = 8 ms to serialize.

definition: The time taken for a signal to travel along a physical path, distinct from serialization, queueing and endpoint processing. It depends on actual route length and propagation speed in the medium.
example: For a hypothetical 5,600 km path and 200,000 km/s signal speed, the one-way propagation component is 28 ms.

definition: TLS version 1.3, specified in RFC 8446. A conventional full handshake uses one round trip without retry, while eligible resumed connections can send replay-sensitive early data; client authentication, retries and application timing qualify end-to-end costs.
example: A new HTTPS connection costs one RTT for TCP plus one for TLS 1.3.

definition: The TLS client's initial handshake message advertising supported parameters and extensions. ServerHello is a distinct server message selecting parameters; TLS 1.3 key shares and retry behaviour follow the negotiated protocol rules.
example: A TLS 1.3 server can send HelloRetryRequest if the offered key share is unsuitable.

definition: A TCP extension (RFC 7413) that lets a client which has a cookie from an earlier connection send data in its SYN, saving a round trip. The data may be replayed, so only safe requests should use it.
example: With TFO, an HTTP request can ride in the SYN and the response can start one RTT sooner.

definition: A 1997 approximation of Reno-style TCP throughput: about MSS divided by RTT, times 1.22 divided by the square root of the loss rate. It shows why long paths need very low loss.
example: With a 1,460-byte MSS, 100 ms RTT and 0.01% loss it gives about 14 Mbit/s.

definition: The fraction of packets that are lost, written p in formulas: 0.0001 means one in ten thousand.
example: Cutting the loss rate from 0.04% to 0.01% doubles the Mathis estimate.

definition: A path with both high bandwidth and long RTT, so its bandwidth-delay product is large and a single flow needs a big window and very low loss to fill it.
example: A 10 Gbit/s transatlantic link with 80 ms RTT is a long fat pipe holding 100 MB in flight.

definition: Excessive persistent queueing that raises latency under load, often associated with oversized or poorly managed buffers. A packet waiting behind 256 KiB at a fixed 2 Mbit/s service rate waits about a second, but other queues and scheduling classes can differ.
example: A packet behind 256 KiB in a fixed-rate 2 Mbit/s FIFO waits about a second before its own transmission; other queues or priority classes can differ.

definition: Time a packet waits in a queue before its own service starts. For a fixed-rate FIFO with no intervening scheduling changes, its queued work ahead divided by service rate gives that wait; priorities or changing rates require a different model.
example: 500,000 queued bytes on a 10 Mbit/s link add 0.4 s of queueing delay.

definition: First in, first out: a queue that serves items strictly in arrival order. In a router this means every new packet waits behind the whole backlog.
example: In a FIFO, a voice packet arriving behind 1 MB of upload data waits for all of it.

definition: A queue policy accepting packets while capacity is available and dropping arrivals when that capacity is exhausted. It supplies no early signal by itself; other ECN/AQM mechanisms can coexist with an ultimate tail-drop limit.
example: A pure tail-drop FIFO can maintain a standing queue during sustained load.

definition: A queue that remains nonempty persistently rather than absorbing a brief burst and draining. Its occupancy adds waiting time; whether a particular delay triggers CoDel depends on sustained sojourn time, its interval and its remaining-backlog check.
example: Persistent 30–40 ms sojourn time can satisfy CoDel's signalling conditions when sufficient backlog remains.

definition: Active queue management: queue algorithms that drop or ECN-mark packets early, before the buffer fills, to keep queueing delay low.
example: CoDel and fq_codel are AQM algorithms.

definition: Controlled Delay: an AQM algorithm that measures how long packets wait (their sojourn time) and starts dropping or marking when the minimum wait stays above a target (usually 5 ms) for an interval (usually 100 ms).
example: A queue that empties within 20 ms is left alone; one stuck above 5 ms for 100 ms starts being signalled.

definition: How long a packet spends in a queue, from arrival to departure. CoDel measures it directly instead of counting bytes.
example: A packet that waits 12 ms in a router queue has a 12 ms sojourn time.

definition: Flow Queue CoDel, combining hash-based flow queues, a modified deficit round-robin scheduler and per-queue CoDel. It reduces bulk/sparse flow interference, while hash collisions, packet sizes and shared bottlenecks prevent absolute isolation or latency guarantees.
example: A managed router using fq_codel can improve latency under upload load, but the bottleneck location and configuration matter.

definition: Separating flows into queues and scheduling among them to reduce interference. Hash-based implementations can put different flows in one queue, so isolation and equal resource shares are not absolute guarantees.
example: fq_codel reduces bulk-flow interference, while a hash collision can still share a queue.

definition: A fair scheduling method that visits each queue in turn and lets it send up to a byte allowance (quantum), carrying unused allowance forward, so flows get fair shares even with different packet sizes.
example: fq_codel uses a modified deficit round-robin to choose which flow queue sends next.

aliases: Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput
definition: Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput: an architecture combining scalable congestion control (such as DCTCP-like algorithms) with ECN marking and AQM to keep queueing delay very low.
example: L4S traffic uses a separate ECN codepoint so routers can mark it at shallow queue depths.

definition: Controlling the rate of transmitted traffic, commonly by queueing data and releasing it under a rate/burst policy. Shaping below an inaccessible bottleneck can move queueing to a managed router, but the required margin and throughput trade-off need measurement.
example: Shaping below a measured inaccessible bottleneck can move sustained queueing to a controlled router; a suggested 95% setting needs measurement and may not fit variable-rate links.

definition: The way deployed middleboxes' assumptions about how a protocol looks make it hard to change: anything new or unusual risks being dropped or rewritten.
example: A firewall that drops SYNs with unfamiliar options helps ossify TCP.

definition: Multipath TCP: an extension that spreads one connection over several paths, such as Wi-Fi and mobile data, falling back to ordinary TCP when the path does not support it.
example: A phone using MPTCP can keep a download going when it moves from Wi-Fi to 5G.

definition: Sending application data in the very first flight of a resumed TLS 1.3 or QUIC connection, with no round trip of waiting. The data can be replayed by an attacker, so it must be safe to repeat.
example: A returning client can send an idempotent GET as 0-RTT data.

definition: In QUIC, an identifier carried in packets that names the connection independently of IP addresses and ports, so a connection can survive an address change.
example: When a phone's address changes, the server still recognises its packets by their connection ID.

definition: Moving a QUIC connection onto a changed network path while retaining connection state. Active migration requires confirmed handshake state and appropriate connection IDs, is subject to negotiated restrictions, and validates a new path while limiting unvalidated sending; continuation is conditional rather than guaranteed.
example: A validated, reachable 5G path can allow eligible QUIC connection continuation after Wi-Fi disappears.

definition: QUIC’s PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE exchange tests reachability on a path using unpredictable echoed data. It is one form of address validation; connection establishment can validate an address through handshake or token rules instead, and sending on an unvalidated path is restricted.
example: Before sending much data to a migrated client, a QUIC server validates the new path.

definition: A counter identifying a QUIC transmission within one packet-number space; a new transmission uses a new increasing number even when resending stream data. A packet-number space is a separate numbering and acknowledgement context: Initial, Handshake and Application Data use three such spaces.
example: If packet 7's data is lost and resent, it goes out as packet 12, so its ACK is unambiguous.

definition: In QUIC, the position of data within one stream, kept separately from packet numbers, so resent data keeps its place in the stream.
example: Bytes 0 to 999 of a stream keep offsets 0 to 999 however many times they are resent.

definition: A typed unit of content inside an encrypted QUIC packet. STREAM frames carry application bytes; ACK, flow-control and other control frames manage the connection. One packet can hold several frames.
example: A single QUIC packet might carry an ACK frame and a STREAM frame together.

definition: QUIC masking of selected header bits and the packet number in addition to packet-payload protection. Keys for Initial packets are publicly derivable, so Initial protection does not hide this information from a capable observer.
example: An observer can derive QUIC Initial keys; later protected packet numbers have different confidentiality assumptions.

definition: An optional QUIC latency spin bit in eligible short headers, used by an observer to estimate round-trip time from transitions. Endpoint disabling, loss, reordering, sampling and traffic patterns limit the inference.
example: Regular spin transitions can support a path RTT estimate without decrypting payloads; they are not guaranteed one-for-one latency measurements.

definition: Accurate ECN: TCP feedback specified in RFC 9768 (2026), using a small cumulative CE-packet counter and optional byte counters for the received ECN codepoints. It supports finer feedback than classic RFC 3168; original DCTCP uses its own modified ECE signalling and does not require AccECN.
example: With AccECN, a receiver can report that 3 of the last 10 packets were marked.

definition: An HTTP/2 frame type that carries a stream's body bytes. gRPC puts its own length-prefixed messages inside DATA frames.
example: A 50 KB response body may travel as several HTTP/2 DATA frames.

definition: A Linux setting (default 1) that shrinks a connection's congestion window after it has been idle for longer than its RTO, so a reused connection does not burst a stale large window.
example: With the default, a keep-alive connection that sits idle for several RTOs has its congestion window cut back, so its next burst starts much smaller.

definition: The standard set of calls (socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, close) that programs use for network communication, from 1980s BSD Unix. Python's socket module wraps it.
example: A Python server calls bind(), listen() and accept() from the socket API.

definition: The socket call that turns a bound socket into a listening socket in the LISTEN state, ready to accept connections; its argument sets the size of the accept queue.
example: srv.listen(128) asks for an accept queue of up to 128 completed connections.

definition: A call returning a separate connected socket for a pending connection. In ordinary TCP the kernel completes establishment before acceptance; TCP Fast Open can allow acceptance sooner. The listening socket remains available.
example: conn, addr = srv.accept() returns the next client's socket and address.

definition: A call receiving available socket data. A positive-size stream read can return fewer bytes than requested; with no local receive shutdown, empty bytes after prior data is consumed indicate stream EOF. Zero-length reads and datagram sockets need different interpretation.
example: recv(4096) may return 3 bytes if only 3 have arrived.

definition: The socket call that hands data to the kernel for sending. It may accept only part of the buffer and returns how many bytes it took; the rest must be sent again.
example: On a non-blocking socket, send() of 100 KB might return 65,536.

definition: A Python socket method that keeps calling send() until the whole buffer has been accepted by the kernel, or raises an error. Success means local acceptance, not delivery to the peer.
example: sock.sendall(header + body) sends both pieces in full on a blocking socket.

definition: The call that releases a socket descriptor. When the last reference closes, TCP normally sends FIN for a graceful close (or RST if unread data or SO_LINGER 0 says so).
example: conn.close() after a response starts the server's side of the close.

definition: The kernel's queue of fully established connections waiting for the application to call accept(). Its size is set by listen()'s backlog, capped by somaxconn.
example: If a server stops calling accept(), its accept queue fills and new handshakes stall.

definition: The number passed to listen() that sets how many completed connections may wait in the accept queue, subject to the system cap.
example: listen(128) requests a backlog of 128, capped by net.core.somaxconn.

definition: The Linux setting that caps the listen backlog any socket can request; its default is 4,096 since Linux 5.4 (128 before).
example: Even if a program calls listen(10000), Linux limits the accept queue to somaxconn.
