definition: A Linux counter associated with listen-queue overload handling. A rise warrants examining queue occupancy, arrival bursts, acceptance and resource limits; it does not uniquely prove one slow handler or a particular packet sequence.
example: Rising overflow counts prompt measurement of listen queues, arrivals, accept scheduling and resource limits.

definition: A Linux option controlling reset behaviour when a listening service cannot accept quickly enough. Default zero can permit a later recovery path that ignores a final ACK; one enables aborting overload cases, and other drop paths also exist.
example: With tcp_abort_on_overflow = 0, one accept-overflow path can ignore the final ACK and allow later recovery; other overload paths may still drop attempts.

definition: Where one application message ends and the next begins. UDP keeps them (one datagram per message); TCP does not, so applications must add their own framing.
example: Two TCP sends of 5 bytes may arrive as one 10-byte read, losing the boundary between them.

definition: How a receiver finds where one unit of data ends and the next begins. At the link layer it is the frame format (header, payload and error check); for an application protocol over TCP's byte stream it is the rule that marks message boundaries: a length prefix, a delimiter or end of stream.
example: HTTP/1.1 headers end at a blank line; body framing then follows method/status rules, transfer coding, Content-Length or closure.

definition: A framing method where each message starts with a fixed-size number giving its length, so the receiver knows exactly how many bytes to read.
example: A 4-byte prefix 00 00 00 03 followed by abc frames a 3-byte message.

definition: A marker byte sequence that ends each message in a stream, such as \r\n; the receiver buffers data until it finds one.
example: SMTP commands and HTTP/1.1 header lines each end with the delimiter \r\n.

definition: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the protocol mail servers use to send email over TCP, with commands and replies as text lines ending in \r\n.
example: A mail client sends MAIL FROM, RCPT TO and DATA commands over SMTP.

definition: An HTTP field expressing a selected representation or message-content length in bytes, with version/method/status-specific framing rules. For example, a HEAD response may describe a body length without actually carrying that body.
example: Content-Length: 512 on an ordinary body-bearing response describes 512 bytes, while HEAD follows special rules.

definition: An HTTP/1.1 way to send a body whose size is not known in advance, as a series of chunks each preceded by its length, ending with a zero-length chunk.
example: A server streaming a generated report uses chunked encoding.

definition: End of file or stream: no further bytes will be read in that direction. For an ordinary TCP socket with positive read size and no local receive shutdown, empty bytes after buffered data is consumed indicate peer sending-direction closure; a zero-size read is a separate case.
example: A recv(4096) that returns b"" has reached EOF.

definition: A read returning fewer bytes than requested, or by the associated aliases a write accepting fewer bytes than supplied. Ordinary sockets permit both; code needing an exact amount must retain and retry the remainder while handling EOF, errors and deadlines.
example: A recv(4) returning two bytes does not prove the remaining two are lost; they may arrive later.

definition: A socket mode in which operations may wait for progress instead of immediately reporting would-block. A read can still be short, a write can be partial, and errors, timeouts or EOF can end the wait; blocking does not mean a whole application message is transferred.
example: A blocking recv() on a silent connection waits indefinitely unless a timeout is set.

definition: A socket mode in which an operation that cannot progress reports would-block rather than waiting for future data or buffer space. A call can still be partial or fail; CPU work, scheduling and documented platform exceptions mean this is not a promise of zero elapsed time.
example: s.setblocking(False) makes recv() raise BlockingIOError when no data is ready.

definition: A Python OSError subclass for an operation that cannot complete immediately, including non-blocking socket would-block or connection-in-progress cases. Corresponding error codes include EAGAIN, EWOULDBLOCK, EALREADY and EINPROGRESS.
example: A non-blocking send() with a full send buffer raises BlockingIOError.

definition: An operating-system interface (select, poll, epoll, kqueue) that tells a program which of many sockets can be read or written without blocking, so one thread can serve them all.
example: An event loop asks the readiness API which sockets have data, then reads only those.

definition: The original readiness calls: you pass a set of descriptors and they report which are ready. select() scans up to the highest descriptor number and poll() the descriptors you pass, so both slow down with many sockets.
example: With the common fd_set interface, select() is limited by FD_SETSIZE (usually 1,024 on Linux); poll() can accept larger descriptor sets but scans the submitted entries.

definition: Linux's readiness API using an interest list and a ready list rather than requiring an application to resubmit every watched descriptor each wait. It scales well for many idle descriptors, but registration, ready events, locking and actual I/O still have costs.
example: An event loop using epoll can watch 50,000 mostly idle connections with one thread.

definition: The readiness and event-notification API on BSD systems and macOS, playing the same role as Linux's epoll.
example: Python's selectors module uses kqueue on macOS.

definition: Python's standard module wrapping the platform's best readiness API (epoll, kqueue, poll or select) behind one interface.
example: selectors.DefaultSelector() picks epoll on Linux.

definition: A single thread that repeatedly asks which sockets or timers are ready and runs the code for each, so many connections share one thread without blocking.
example: asyncio runs an event loop that serves thousands of connections from one thread.

definition: Python's standard library for writing event-loop programs with async and await, so concurrent network code reads like sequential code.
example: asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 9002) starts an event-loop TCP server.

definition: An asyncio stream method that pauses the coroutine when the transport's write buffer is above its high watermark, until it drains to the low watermark. It is how asyncio code applies backpressure.
example: Awaiting writer.drain() after each bounded write makes the coroutine respect transport backpressure; application message sizes and deadlines still need limits.

definition: A buffer-size threshold: above the high watermark, writing is paused; below the low watermark, it resumes.
example: With a 64 KiB high watermark, a transport can pause its producer after the buffer exceeds that threshold; one large write can overshoot it.

definition: A server design that starts a separate thread for every client. Simple to write, but each thread costs memory and scheduling, which limits scale to many mostly idle connections.
example: A thread-per-connection server comfortable at 50 clients may struggle at 50,000.

definition: A small integer the operating system gives a process to refer to an open file or socket. Each process has a limit on how many it may hold.
example: A process with a 1,024-descriptor limit can hold at most about 1,024 open sockets.

definition: A socket option relaxing platform-specific local address-reuse rules. It can help a restarted listener bind despite retained TCP connection state, but active-listener conflicts and old/new socket settings still matter; it is distinct from SO_REUSEPORT.
example: socket.create_server sets SO_REUSEADDR on POSIX systems.

definition: A socket option (Linux 3.9+) that lets several sockets listen on the same address and port, each with its own accept queue; the kernel spreads new connections among them.
example: Eight Nginx workers each open their own listener on port 443 with SO_REUSEPORT.

definition: Portable Operating System Interface: the family of standards for Unix-like operating systems' APIs, including sockets, followed by Linux and macOS.
example: Socket option names such as SO_REUSEADDR come from POSIX.

definition: Berkeley Packet Filter: a way to run small, verified programs inside the Linux kernel. With SO_REUSEPORT it can choose which listener gets each new connection.
example: A BPF program can steer connections to SO_REUSEPORT listeners by CPU.

definition: The user identity a process's permissions are checked against. Linux only lets sockets share a port with SO_REUSEPORT if they have the same effective user ID.
example: Two server processes run as the same user can share a port with SO_REUSEPORT.

definition: Big-endian byte order, with the most significant byte first, the standard order for numbers in network protocol headers.
example: The number 3 as a 4-byte big-endian integer is 00 00 00 03.

definition: Python's module for converting between Python values and packed binary data; "!I" means one 4-byte unsigned integer in network byte order.
example: struct.unpack("!I", b"\x00\x00\x00\x03") returns (3,).

definition: The Python exception raised when a connection attempt is answered with RST, usually because nothing is listening on the port.
example: socket.create_connection(("localhost", 9)) raises ConnectionRefusedError if no service runs there.

definition: The Python exception raised when the peer aborts an established connection with RST.
example: Reading from a socket whose peer crashed and rebooted can raise ConnectionResetError.

definition: The Python exception raised when writing to a connection that can no longer send, for example after the peer has reset it.
example: Writing to a socket after the peer reset the connection can raise BrokenPipeError.

definition: The Python exception raised when a socket operation exceeds the timeout set with settimeout(); socket.timeout is an older name for it.
example: With conn.settimeout(5), a recv() that waits more than 5 seconds raises TimeoutError.

definition: A Python exception meaning input ended unexpectedly. The lesson's recv_exact raises it when the peer closes in the middle of a message.
example: If the peer closes after 2 bytes of a 4-byte header, recv_exact raises EOFError.

definition: Global interpreter lock: a lock limiting Python bytecode execution to one thread at a time in GIL-enabled CPython builds. Blocking I/O releases it; optional free-threaded CPython builds have different execution and extension-compatibility rules.
example: A GIL-enabled CPython thread waiting in recv does not prevent another Python thread from running.

definition: The standard, reference implementation of Python, written in C; it is what 'python' usually means.
example: python3 on most systems is CPython.

definition: A widely used web server and reverse proxy that serves many connections from a few worker processes using event loops.
example: Nginx with 8 workers can use SO_REUSEPORT so each worker has its own listener.

definition: A Python thread marked so that it does not keep the process alive. The program exits when no non-daemon threads remain, and daemon threads can be stopped abruptly without orderly cleanup.
example: threading.Thread(target=handle, daemon=True) creates a daemon thread per connection.

definition: A scheme that makes a client solve a costly puzzle before a server spends resources on it. TCP has no such mechanism; SYN cookies need no client changes.
example: A proof-of-work puzzle might require finding a hash with 20 leading zero bits.

definition: A command-line tool for making HTTP and other network requests, often used to test servers.
example: curl -v https://example.com shows the connection setup and response headers.

definition: Handing work such as checksums or splitting large buffers into segments to the network card or a lower layer, to save CPU.
example: With segmentation offload, the kernel passes a 64 KB buffer to the NIC, which cuts it into 1,460-byte segments.

definition: The smallest unit of data, a single 0 or 1. Network speeds are quoted in bits per second; eight bits make one byte.
example: A 1,500-byte packet is 12,000 bits.

definition: Kilobits per second: thousands of bits per second.
example: 32 kbit/s is 32,000 bits per second.

definition: Kibibyte: exactly 1,024 bytes (2^10).
example: 256 KiB = 262,144 bytes.

definition: Megabyte: a million bytes (10^6). MB/s means megabytes per second; multiply by 8 for Mbit/s.
example: 12.5 MB is 100 megabits.

definition: Mebibyte: exactly 1,048,576 bytes (2^20).
One millionth of a second (µs).
example: RFC 9293 discusses an ISN clock that ticks about every 4 µs.

definition: Sending data again because it seems to have been lost. TCP resends the same bytes with their original sequence numbers, triggered by duplicate ACKs, SACK or RACK evidence, or the retransmission timer.
example: When segment 1001 is lost, the sender retransmits bytes 1001 to 2000 after three duplicate ACKs.

definition: A transfer for which setup, request round trips or early congestion-window growth can dominate latency when capacity is sufficient. Size alone does not guarantee this: serialization, endpoint work, loss and limits can dominate instead.
example: The five-RTT 100,000-byte example assumes ideal flights, enough link capacity and negligible processing/serialization.

definition: Cryptographic assurance of a peer's claimed identity under a protocol's validation rules, such as certificate and hostname validation in TLS. A TCP handshake exchanges sequence state and does not supply such identity proof.
example: A successful TCP handshake is insufficient evidence that the endpoint is the intended HTTPS server.

definition: The information an endpoint (or a stateful middlebox) keeps about each connection. A TCP endpoint keeps it in a transmission control block (TCB): addresses and ports, the current state, sequence numbers, windows and timers.
example: TIME_WAIT keeps a stripped-down copy of the connection state so a repeated FIN can still be acknowledged.

definition: The endpoint responding to the first FIN in an ordinary sequential graceful TCP close. It can continue sending in CLOSE_WAIT before sending its own FIN and waiting in LAST_ACK; simultaneous closure has different event ordering.
The TLS server handshake message selecting negotiated parameters. It is distinct from the client's ClientHello; TLS 1.3 can use a specially encoded HelloRetryRequest when a retry is needed.

The TCP control bit indicating that this segment's acknowledgement field is significant. A set flag validates the field's role; it does not mean the segment carries no data or that a peer application processed the acknowledged bytes.
example: SYN+ACK carries both the SYN and ACK control bits, with the acknowledgement covering the peer's SYN.
